entities.name: Mut'im ibn Adi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Muṭʽim ibn ʽAdi (died 623 CE) was a prominent chieftain of the Banu Nawfal clan, a significant lineage within the powerful Banu Quraish tribe of Mecca during the early 7th century CE. His historical importance stems from his pivotal, albeit non-Muslim, role in protecting the nascent Islamic community and its prophet, Muhammad, during a critical period of persecution in Mecca. As a respected elder and a man of considerable influence, Muṭʽim operated within the complex tribal politics of pre-Islamic Arabia, where alliances and pledges of protection (jiwar) were paramount to survival, especially for those lacking strong clan support. His actions directly impacted the Prophet's ability to continue his mission in Mecca, particularly after the deaths of Khadijah and Abu Talib, which left Muhammad vulnerable.

Muṭʽim's most celebrated intervention occurred around 619-620 CE, following the 'Year of Sorrow' and the Prophet Muhammad's unsuccessful mission to Ta'if. Upon Muhammad's return to Mecca, facing severe hostility and lacking the protection previously afforded by his uncle Abu Talib, Muṭʽim publicly granted him safe passage (jiwar) into the city. This act involved Muṭʽim and his sons standing armed at the Kaaba, declaring Muhammad under their protection, thereby deterring further aggression from other Quraish factions. Earlier, during the three-year boycott of the Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muṭṭalib (c. 616-619 CE), Muṭʽim was also instrumental in mobilizing support to annul the unjust embargo, demonstrating his consistent opposition to the extreme persecution of Muhammad and his followers.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Mut'im ibn Adi's protection of the Prophet Muhammad was a critical turning point, directly enabling the Prophet's continued mission in Mecca after the 'Year of Sorrow' and contributing to the conditions that led to the Hijra, thereby significantly impacting the foundation of Islam.
